newsitem.title: USA: Texas electric deregulation bill moves toward vote.
newsitem.headline: Texas electric deregulation bill moves toward vote.

text.p: A compromise bill to deregulate the electric power industry in Texas faced a critical committee vote over the weekend as opponents lined up against the proposal, lobbyists said Friday.

The House State Affairs committee convened a hearing late Friday and must sign off on the bill by Saturday to get the proposal on the House calendar in the final weeks of the legislative session, lobbyists said.
"I think we have a go," said Bill Miller, a lobbyist for the Texas Coalition for Competitive Electricity, which represents large industrial power customers.

The current House proposal would open markets to competition on January 1, 2002, cut residential rates by 10 percent, freeze commercial rates and allow utilities to recover stranded costs by depreciation and securitization.
The bill must move out of committee by Saturday or the plug could be pulled on any deregulation efforts in Texas, where the legislature adjourns its biennial session June 2.

"The problem with Texas is if the legislature doesn't do anything this year, they don't come back into session for two years," said Bill Rockford, a managing director with Chase Securities Inc's global power and environmental group.

Houston-based Enron Corp, the nation's leading electric wholesaler, opposed a delay until 2002 for opening the market and sought assurances it would have a level playing field with utilities once retail competition begins.

"(The bill) still doesn't have language in it that we think would be essential for consumers having real choices, in its current form," Enron lobbyist Steve Kean said. "We want a toehold in here, and if we get a toehold we will do our best to give consumers real choices."

An earlier Senate bill died after investor-owned utilities, power marketers and industrial customers failed to reach agreement on two key issues -- stranded cost recovery and a deadline for opening local markets to competition.

Texas has emerged as a key state in the domestic deregulated electric industry as Houston-based natural gas companies leverage their trading expertise and back-room investments to form national electric wholesale operations.
But the state, which opened its grid to wholesale competition two years ago, could lag the nation in electric retail competition if the House bill dies, lobbyists said.
"We would rather see no legislation than bad legislation," Enron's Kean said.
